title: Find the game's two secret numbers with gdb and store them in input.txt
successMessage: Your file matched the expected output
notes: observed -- the README's only deliverable is `create a file called input.txt and place them in that file, one per line (round 1's secret number on the first line, and round 2's on the second line)`; 10_gdb/input.txt (20 bytes, the submission that passed) holds exactly those two lines. re/original-grade-txt/10_gdb.grade.txt is byte-identical to the 00_hello and 01_apple reports apart from the timestamp -- all three bodies hash to f9cbea38ba10020526bc9199bca4f53c -- and, unlike every run-based assignment in the workspace, it contains no compile or run line at all, i.e. the original grader took the same path as its two plain file comparisons. recovered -- the shipped Linux x86-64 `game` binary is the independent key to what the right numbers are. It is not stripped; re/elf/10_gdb__game.md (generated with tools/re/elfdump.py) records its symbol table (getSecretNumber at 0x400890, 6 bytes; getOtherSN at 0x4008a0, 22 bytes), its `.rodata` strings and its disassembly, in which getSecretNumber is `movl $0x1badf00d, %eax; retq` (= 464384013, line 1) and getOtherSN is `srand(which); return random();` (calls srand@plt then tail-jumps to random@plt). That binary was built on Ubuntu 14.04 with gcc 4.8.4 -- older than the gcc 9.3.0 of the workspace's other objects -- but glibc's random() has been the same additive-feedback generator (TYPE_3: 31-entry state, separation 3, 310 values discarded after seeding) throughout. Re-implementing it and XOR-ing getOtherSN(i) for i = 0..5678 reproduces 938257400 exactly (line 2); the host's own random() does not, which is why the numbers are recovered rather than recomputed. inferred -- that the stored expected blob is compared byte-for-byte, so a differently formatted but behaviourally usable input.txt would fail here just as it would have in 2024; nothing in the artifact proves the original did not instead run `./game < input.txt`. drivers/10_gdb/game_secrets.c carries the recovered getSecretNumber/getOtherSN pair so the fixture can be re-derived, and would be the driver if the check were ever changed to a behavioural one. Note also that gdb does not exist on this platform, so the assignment's intended tool is unavailable even though its deliverable is still gradable.
